openingProblem.problem: In 1945 all four occupying powers said they wanted a single Germany. By 1949 there were two German states, and by 1955 each was armed and in a rival alliance. Who divided Germany: Moscow, the West, or the Germans themselves?
openingProblem.predictionPrompt: Your prediction in one line: who was most responsible for dividing Germany?
openingProblem.revisitPrompt: Look back at your prediction. Which piece of evidence most changed or confirmed it?

chunks.title: Potsdam and the occupation, 1945–1946
chunks.body:
At Potsdam, between 17 July and 2 August 1945, Stalin, Truman and Churchill (replaced midway by Attlee) agreed what to do with defeated Germany, but only in general terms. Germany would be divided into zones of occupation; Germans would be expelled from eastern Europe; and the occupiers would pursue "democratization", "denazification" and "decartelization". Tony Judt points out the contradiction at the heart of the deal. Germany was to be treated as a single economic unit, yet the Soviet Union was allowed to take goods and equipment from its own zone and 10 per cent of reparations from the Western zones. Reparations, as after 1918, divided the victors from the start.

The early American aim was to punish and weaken. Policy rested on demilitarisation, denazification and deindustrialisation: the Wehrmacht was formally dissolved on 20 August 1946, and a plan of March 1946 strictly limited German industry, especially steel.

That approach soon looked absurd to the Western occupiers. Germany could not feed itself. By July 1946 Britain had imported 112,000 tons of wheat and 50,000 tons of potatoes for its zone, paid for with an American loan; the occupation cost Britain $80 million a year against at most $29 million in reparations, while bread was rationed at home for the first time. Chancellor Hugh Dalton complained that Britain was "paying reparations to the Germans". The Americans and British also feared that hungry, hopeless Germans would turn back to Nazism or to Communism, so they began handing Germans responsibility for their own affairs.

The Soviet zone went the other way. From the outset the Soviets set up a Communist-led administration and dismantled factories for shipment east. Communism had little appeal: in the Berlin elections of 20 October 1946 the Communists came far behind both the Social Democrats and the Christian Democrats.

The first parting came in 1946. In May the US military governor, General Lucius Clay, suspended reparations from the American zone, saying the Soviets had broken their Potsdam undertakings; Britain followed two months later. On 6 September 1946, in a speech at Stuttgart, Secretary of State James Byrnes promised that the US Army would stay in Germany as long as an occupation was needed. This mattered because the Western powers now saw German recovery as their interest, which meant that the Potsdam idea of a single, weakened Germany was already breaking down.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Potsdam's contradictions over reparations divided the victors from the start.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: All four powers still formally accepted a single Germany in 1946, so division was not yet decided.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The cost of occupation pushed Britain and the US towards German recovery.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Fear of Communism and Nazism, not only cost, shaped the change.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Soviet policy in its zone made Communism unattractive to Germans.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Stalin had little choice: Communists could not win by votes.

howItGetsAsked: Compare and contrast Soviet and Western policies towards Germany between 1945 and 1949.
Discuss the view that the Western powers, not the Soviet Union, were responsible for the division of Germany.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The Western powers abandoned the Potsdam aim of a weakened Germany because occupation was ruinously expensive.
useItInAnEssay.prove: By July 1946 Britain was importing wheat and potatoes for its zone and paying $80 million a year against at most $29 million in reparations, while rationing bread at home.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that a weak Germany was a burden on its occupiers, so in May 1946 Clay suspended reparations and the Western zones moved towards recovery.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, Soviet dismantling and the Communist-led administration in the East also broke the Potsdam framework.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Cost was therefore the main reason for the Western shift, while Soviet policy made it easier to justify.

chunks.title: The road to division, 1947–1948
chunks.body:
The Western zones began to merge. At the end of 1946 Britain and the United States agreed to combine the economies of their zones in a "Bizone". This did not yet mean a divided Germany: in February 1947 Britain and France signed the Dunkirk Treaty, pledging mutual support against any future *German* aggression, and US Secretary of State George Marshall still hoped for a united German economy.

The real break came at the Moscow conference of Foreign Ministers, from 10 March to 24 April 1947. Britain and the US were now determined to rebuild the western German economy so that Germans could support themselves and help European recovery. The Soviet Union wanted reparations from the Western zones and a united German administration. But a single German administration, Judt explains, would have meant in practice handing the country to the Soviet sphere, given the Red Army's military superiority. Robert Murphy, the American political adviser in Germany, said it was the Moscow conference "which really rang down the Iron Curtain".

Events then moved fast. On 23 May 1947 the Bizone gained a German Economic Council, the embryo of a West German government. The US directive JCS 1067, with its punitive aims, was replaced by JCS 1779, which aimed at the economic unification of the western zones and German self-government. "For the Americans especially," Judt writes, "Germans were rapidly ceasing to be the enemy." The last meeting of the four Foreign Ministers, in London in November and December 1947, broke up without agreement and without setting another date.

From 23 February 1948 Britain, France and the US met in London to plan Germany's future. They agreed to extend the Marshall Plan to western Germany and to prepare a West German government, with France's agreement bought by the temporary separation of the Saar and international oversight of the Ruhr. The Soviet representative, Marshal Sokolovsky, protested. On 20 March 1948 he walked out of the Allied Control Council in Berlin; no further meeting was ever held. On 1 April Soviet authorities began to interfere with traffic between the Western zones and Berlin.

The final step was money. On 18 June 1948 the Western powers announced a new currency, the **Deutsche Mark**; three days later it was in circulation. Each German could exchange 40 old Reichsmarks at 1:1 and the rest at 10:1. The reform wiped out savings, but goods quickly reappeared in the shops. This mattered because a separate currency created a separate economy, which meant that the western zones were now, in practice, a separate state in the making.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Moscow conference of 1947 showed that East and West wanted incompatible Germanies.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Both sides still talked of unity for years afterwards.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Western economic decisions, the Bizone, Marshall aid and the Deutsche Mark, created a separate western Germany.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Soviet dismantling and a Communist-led zone had already divided the economy.

argumentsThatWork.claim: For the US, Germans were ceasing to be the enemy by 1947.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: France still feared Germany and had to be bought off with the Saar and the Ruhr.

useItInAnEssay.claim: The currency reform of June 1948 was the decisive economic step towards a separate West German state.
useItInAnEssay.prove: On 18 June the Western powers announced the Deutsche Mark, and three days later it was in circulation, with savings exchanged at 1:1 for the first 40 Reichsmarks and 10:1 thereafter.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that the western zones now had their own economy and currency, so Germany could no longer be run as the single economic unit Potsdam had promised.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, Soviet dismantling and the Communist-led administration in the East had already broken that unity in practice.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The currency reform therefore made division official, rather than creating it from nothing.

chunks.title: Blockade, airlift and two German states, 1948–1949
chunks.body:
The Soviet response came at once. On 23 June 1948 the Soviets issued their own East German mark and cut the railway lines linking Berlin to western Germany; later they closed the canals too. West Berlin, deep inside the Soviet zone, was cut off. The Western commanders refused to let the new Eastern currency circulate in their sectors, and on 26 June the first American transport plane landed at Tempelhof airfield.

The **Berlin airlift** lasted until 12 May 1949. In eleven months the Western allies flew in some 2.3 million tons of food on 277,500 flights; 73 Allied airmen died. Judt explains Stalin's aim: to force the West either to leave Berlin, since the Potsdam agreements gave no written guarantee of road or rail access, or to abandon the plan for a West German state. Berlin was always a bargaining chip for him. He got neither.

The blockade backfired. Coming soon after the Communist coup in Prague, it made the Western powers more determined to create a West German state and made division more acceptable to Germans themselves. In April 1949 France joined the Bizone, creating a western economic unit of 49 million people against 17 million in the Soviet zone. Judt argues that the blockade was an improvisation rather than a plan for aggression: Stalin was not going to war for Berlin. When it failed he changed tack, and on 12 May 1949 he lifted the blockade in return for nothing more than a conference of Foreign Ministers.

That conference achieved nothing. While it met, the Parliamentary Council in Bonn put the **Basic Law** into effect in May 1949, creating the Federal Republic of Germany. The Allies kept some powers, but military government gave way to civilian High Commissioners. After the Christian Democrats' election success, Konrad Adenauer became the first Chancellor on 15 September 1949. Stalin answered by creating the **German Democratic Republic** on 7 October 1949.

Judt's judgement is that the Berlin crisis "led directly to the creation of two German states, an outcome none of the Allies had sought four years earlier". This mattered because a temporary occupation had become a permanent division, which meant that for forty years the German question would be a question of two states, each tied to a bloc.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The blockade failed and accelerated the division it was meant to prevent.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Plans for a West German state existed before the blockade; it confirmed rather than created them.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The airlift showed Western commitment to Berlin and won German opinion.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Stalin was not willing to go to war, so the risk was smaller than it seemed.

argumentsThatWork.claim: By 1949 two German states existed, an outcome no Ally had planned in 1945.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Both sides continued to claim they wanted unity.

howItGetsAsked: Evaluate the causes and consequences of the Berlin blockade of 1948–1949.
To what extent was the Berlin blockade responsible for the division of Germany between 1945 and 1949?

useItInAnEssay.claim: The Berlin blockade backfired because it made the division of Germany more acceptable to the West and to Germans.
useItInAnEssay.prove: The airlift supplied West Berlin for eleven months with 2.3 million tons of food, and in April 1949 France joined the Bizone, creating a western unit of 49 million people.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that Stalin's attempt to stop a West German state instead strengthened Western unity, so the Federal Republic was created in May 1949.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, the plans for a West German state had been agreed in London before the blockade began.
useItInAnEssay.judge: The blockade therefore accelerated division rather than causing it.

chunks.title: Rearmament and sovereignty, 1950–1955
chunks.body:
The Korean War changed the German question. To persuade Congress to fund the defence of Europe, the Americans needed Europeans, including Germans, to contribute. In September 1950 Secretary of State Dean Acheson raised West German rearmament with Britain and France. The French were appalled; NATO, they suspected, was becoming a cover for remilitarising their old enemy. Konrad Adenauer played his hand carefully. Rather than leap at rearmament, he held back and set a price: full international recognition of the Federal Republic and an amnesty for Germans held as war criminals.

To head off a German army, the French Prime Minister René Pleven proposed in October 1950 a **European Defence Community** (EDC), with a European army in which German units would be mixed with others. The treaty was signed on 27 May 1952, and the Bundestag ratified it in March 1953.

The Soviet Union tried to stop it. In a series of **Notes** in the spring of 1952, Stalin proposed a peace treaty creating a united Germany, neutral and demilitarised, with all occupying forces withdrawn and a government chosen in free all-German elections. Some historians have criticised the West for ignoring this "missed opportunity". Judt disagrees: Western leaders were right not to take the Notes seriously, because Moscow itself attached little importance to them. Its aim was to derail the EDC and prevent West German rearmament. The Soviet leaders were in fact not unhappy to see American troops in West Germany as a guarantee against German revival.

The EDC then collapsed in Paris. On 30 August 1954 the French National Assembly rejected it by 319 votes to 264. Prime Minister Pierre Mendès-France explained: "In the EDC there was too much integration and too little England." The answer came within weeks. Britain committed four divisions to the Continent permanently; the Brussels Treaty became the Western European Union; and West Germany could have an army of up to 500,000 and join **NATO** as a sovereign state. In May 1955 the occupation ended and the Federal Republic entered NATO. Ten days later the Soviet Union announced the Warsaw Pact and incorporated the GDR, whose own regime had needed Soviet tanks to crush a workers' rising in June 1953.

This mattered because each German state was now built into a military alliance, which meant that the German question, in Judt's words, "had not exactly been answered", but it would be set aside for a generation.

argumentsThatWork.claim: Rearmament came from the Korean War and American pressure, not German demand.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Adenauer used the demand to win sovereignty, so he shaped the outcome.

argumentsThatWork.claim: The Stalin Notes aimed to stop rearmament, not to unite Germany.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Some historians see a missed opportunity, so the case is debated.

argumentsThatWork.claim: By 1955 both German states were built into opposing alliances.
argumentsThatWork.strongestCounter: Allied troops remained in West Germany, so sovereignty was limited.

howItGetsAsked: Examine the reasons why West Germany was rearmed and admitted to NATO between 1950 and 1955.
Analyse the significance of the Stalin Notes of 1952 for the German question.

useItInAnEssay.claim: West Germany was rearmed mainly because the Korean War made the United States demand a German contribution to Western defence.
useItInAnEssay.prove: In September 1950 Acheson raised rearmament with Britain and France, and after the EDC failed in August 1954 the Paris agreements let West Germany join NATO with an army of up to 500,000.
useItInAnEssay.explain: This meant that American pressure turned the defeated enemy of 1945 into an ally, so Adenauer could demand sovereignty in return.
useItInAnEssay.test: However, French resistance shaped the form: the EDC was rejected, and Britain had to commit four divisions before France would accept a German army.
useItInAnEssay.judge: Rearmament was therefore driven by Washington, but its terms were set by French fears and Adenauer's bargaining.

misconceptions.wrong: Germany was divided at Potsdam in 1945.
misconceptions.right: Potsdam created **zones of occupation**, not states; two German states appeared only in **1949**.

misconceptions.wrong: The Berlin blockade was a Soviet attempt to start a war.
misconceptions.right: Judt calls it an **improvisation**: Stalin wanted the West to leave Berlin or drop the West German state, and would not go to war.

misconceptions.wrong: West Germany demanded rearmament after the war.
misconceptions.right: The **United States** raised it in 1950 because of the Korean War; Adenauer held back to win sovereignty.

misconceptions.wrong: The Stalin Notes were a genuine offer the West foolishly rejected.
misconceptions.right: That is debated; **Judt** argues Moscow's real aim was to stop West German rearmament.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: To what extent was the Berlin blockade responsible for the division of Germany between 1945 and 1949?

decodeKey.verb: To what extent: judge how far
decodeKey.judgement: How far the blockade, compared with earlier decisions, caused division

modelPlan.thesis: The blockade accelerated division rather than causing it: the decisive steps came earlier, but its failure made a West German state acceptable to the West and to Germans.

arguments.claim: The blockade backfired and hardened Western resolve (named factor first).
Potsdam's contradictions and reparations.
The Moscow conference, the Bizone and Marshall aid.
The Deutsche Mark created a separate economy.

modelPlan.counter: The London plans for a West German state predated the blockade, so it was a response, not a cause.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Would two states have emerged without the blockade? Very probably, since the London plans already existed; so its role was to accelerate.

segments.text: The Berlin blockade accelerated the division of Germany rather than causing it.
The London conference had already agreed in early 1948 to prepare a West German government, and the Deutsche Mark was introduced in June, before the blockade began.
This meant that the blockade was Stalin's response to a division already under way, but its failure made that division more acceptable to the West and to Germans.
However, by uniting the Western powers and bringing France into the Bizone in April 1949, it turned plans into a state within months.
The blockade was therefore a decisive accelerant of division, though not its origin.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: “The Western powers, not the Soviet Union, were responsible for the division of Germany.” Discuss with reference to the period 1945 to 1949.

decodeKey.verb: Discuss: test the claim for and against, then judge
decodeKey.judgement: How far the West, rather than the USSR, caused division

modelPlan.thesis: The claim is partly right: the West took the decisive steps to build a separate state, but it did so because Soviet policy made a united Germany either unworkable or Soviet-dominated.

arguments.claim: For: the West stopped reparations and built the Bizone.
For: the London plans and the Deutsche Mark.
Against: Soviet dismantling and a Communist-led zone.
Against: the blockade and the GDR.

modelPlan.counter: Judt argues a single German administration would have meant handing Germany to the Soviet sphere, so the West's choice was defensive.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Who could have kept Germany united on acceptable terms? Neither, so responsibility was shared.

segments.text: The Western powers took the decisive steps towards division, but responsibility was shared.
In 1946 Clay stopped reparations, Britain and the US created the Bizone, and in June 1948 they introduced the Deutsche Mark.
This meant that the western zones became a separate economy, so a West German state followed naturally.
However, the Soviets had set up a Communist-led administration in their zone from the outset, and Judt argues that a single administration would have handed Germany to the Soviet sphere.
The claim is therefore only partly valid: the West built division, but in response to Soviet policy.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Evaluate the causes and consequences of the Berlin blockade of 1948–1949.

decodeKey.judgement: Which cause mattered most, and which consequence was most significant

modelPlan.thesis: The blockade was caused mainly by Western plans for a West German state, crystallised by the currency reform; its main consequence was to accelerate the creation of two German states.

arguments.claim: Cause: the London plans for a West German state.
Cause: the Deutsche Mark.
Consequence: the airlift and Western unity.
Consequence: two German states in 1949.

modelPlan.counter: Judt calls the blockade an improvisation, so its causes lay in Stalin's opportunism as much as in Western plans.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which consequence lasted longest? Two German states, which survived until 1990.

segments.text: The blockade was caused mainly by Western plans for a separate West German state.
In early 1948 the London conference agreed to prepare a West German government, and on 18 June the Deutsche Mark was announced; on 23 June the Soviets cut the rail links to Berlin.
This meant that Stalin used Berlin as a bargaining chip to force the West to drop its plans or leave the city.
However, Judt argues the blockade was an improvisation rather than a planned aggression, since Stalin would not go to war for Berlin.
The blockade's main consequence was therefore the opposite of its aim: it hastened two German states.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Compare and contrast Soviet and Western policies towards Germany between 1945 and 1949.

decodeKey.verb: Compare and contrast: similarities and differences, explicitly linked

modelPlan.thesis: Both sides claimed to want a united Germany and both built a state in their own image, but they differed fundamentally: the West moved from punishment to recovery, while the Soviets extracted reparations and imposed Communist control.

arguments.claim: Similarity: both proclaimed unity but built separate institutions.
Similarity: both initially sought to punish and weaken Germany.
Difference: Western recovery against Soviet extraction.
Difference: Western self-government against Communist control.

modelPlan.counter: Both acted defensively: each feared the other would control a united Germany.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Which difference mattered most? Recovery versus extraction, which made two economies and then two states.

segments.text: Soviet and Western policies both proclaimed unity, but they pulled Germany in opposite directions.
The West stopped reparations in 1946 and built up its zones' economy, whereas the Soviets dismantled factories and set up a Communist-led administration in their zone.
This meant the two halves developed different economies and political systems, so each side's idea of unity became unacceptable to the other.
However, both began with punitive aims at Potsdam, and both claimed until 1949 that they wanted a single Germany.
The decisive difference was therefore recovery against extraction, which turned zones into states.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Examine the reasons why West Germany was rearmed and admitted to NATO between 1950 and 1955.

decodeKey.verb: Examine: break the issue into parts and consider their interrelationship
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The reasons for rearmament and NATO entry

modelPlan.thesis: West Germany was rearmed mainly because the Korean War made the US demand a German contribution to Western defence; French resistance and Adenauer's bargaining decided the form.

arguments.claim: The Korean War and American pressure.
Adenauer's price: recognition and sovereignty.
The failure of the EDC.
British commitment and the Paris agreements.

modelPlan.counter: The Stalin Notes offered an alternative, but Judt argues it was not serious.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Without which reason would there have been no rearmament? American pressure, since neither France nor Adenauer sought it.

segments.text: West Germany was rearmed mainly because the Korean War made the US demand a German contribution to defence.
In September 1950 Acheson raised rearmament with Britain and France, and after the EDC failed in August 1954, the Paris agreements let West Germany join NATO in May 1955.
This meant that the former enemy became an ally within ten years, because the US needed European troops to justify its own commitment.
However, France rejected the EDC and accepted a German army only after Britain promised four divisions, so French fears shaped the outcome.
American pressure was therefore the decisive reason, while French conditions and Adenauer's bargaining set the terms.

essayQuestions.label: Teacher-constructed practice material. Not an IB publication.
essayQuestions.text: Analyse the significance of the Stalin Notes of 1952 for the German question.

decodeKey.verb: Analyse: break the question into its parts and show how they connect
decodeKey.factorOrTask: The significance of the Stalin Notes
decodeKey.judgement: How much the Notes mattered, and why

modelPlan.thesis: The Notes were significant mainly as evidence of Soviet priorities: Moscow preferred a divided Germany with US troops to a rearmed West Germany, and the West's refusal confirmed that division would continue.

arguments.claim: What the Notes offered.
Their real aim: stopping rearmament and the EDC.
Western rejection and the EDC's signature.
The 'missed opportunity' debate.

modelPlan.counter: Some historians see a genuine missed opportunity to end the Cold War's most dangerous confrontation.
modelPlan.judgementCriterion: Did the Notes change the German question? No, which is itself their significance: they show neither side wanted unity on the other's terms.

segments.text: The Stalin Notes were significant less as an offer than as evidence of what Moscow feared.
In spring 1952 Stalin proposed a united, neutral, demilitarised Germany, just as the EDC Treaty was about to be signed on 27 May 1952.
This meant the Notes were aimed at stopping West German rearmament, and Judt argues Moscow attached little importance to unity itself.
However, some historians criticise the West for missing a chance to remove the most dangerous point of confrontation.
The Notes therefore mattered mainly by confirming that both sides preferred division to the other's version of unity.
